01-01.text: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect, declaring enslaved people in areas in rebellion free.
Texas concealed handgun licenses issued under Senate Bill 60 (1995) took effect.

01-04.text: Presser v. Illinois held the Second Amendment then limited only the national government, not the States.

01-16.text: The Eighteenth Amendment was ratified, establishing national Prohibition of intoxicating liquors.

01-17.text: Benjamin Franklin, signer of the Declaration and the Constitution, was born.

01-21.text: Pearson v. Callahan held the Saucier two-step qualified immunity sequence is not mandatory.

01-23.text: The Twentieth Amendment was ratified, ending presidential terms at noon on January 20.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment was ratified, barring poll taxes in federal elections.
United States v. Jones held attaching a GPS tracker to a vehicle and monitoring it is a Fourth Amendment search.

01-31.text: Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment, which would abolish slavery once ratified by the states.

02-03.text: The Fifteenth Amendment was ratified, barring denial of the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
The Sixteenth Amendment was ratified, allowing Congress to tax incomes without apportionment among the states.

02-07.text: The Eleventh Amendment was ratified, limiting federal court suits against a state by citizens of another state or a foreign country.

02-10.text: The Twenty-fifth Amendment was ratified, addressing presidential succession and disability.

02-15.text: Texas voters ratified the Constitution of 1876, still the state's basic law, by 136,606 to 56,652.

02-16.text: The Mexican army under Santa Anna crossed the Rio Grande, advancing toward San Antonio.

02-19.text: In a transfer ceremony, President Anson Jones declared, "the Republic of Texas is no more."

02-20.text: Congress passed the Twenty-first Amendment to repeal Prohibition.
Timbs v. Indiana, an Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause case, was decided.

02-23.text: Santa Anna's advance force reached San Antonio and the siege of the Alamo began.

02-24.text: William B. Travis wrote his Alamo letter "To the People of Texas and All Americans in the World," vowing "Victory or Death."
Weeks v. United States was decided, the foundational federal exclusionary rule case.
Tinker v. Des Moines, the student armband First Amendment case, was decided.
02-24.case: Tinker v. Des Moines Indep. Community School Dist., 393 U.S. 503 (1969)

02-24.text: Hustler Magazine v. Falwell barred public figures from emotional distress damages for a parody absent actual malice.
02-24.case: Hustler Magazine, Inc. v. Falwell, 485 U.S. 46 (1988)

02-26.text: Congress passed the Fifteenth Amendment protecting the right to vote regardless of race or color.

02-27.text: The Twenty-second Amendment was ratified: no person may be elected President more than twice.

02-28.text: The U.S. Congress passed the joint resolution proposing annexation of Texas.

03-01.text: Maryland ratified the Articles of Confederation, bringing the Congress of the Confederation into being.
The Convention of 1836 met at Washington-on-the-Brazos to consider independence from Mexico.

03-02.text: The Convention of 1836 adopted the Texas Declaration of Independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos.
The original Texas Declaration of Independence was unveiled in a niche at the Texas Capitol.
Congress passed the Twentieth Amendment, which moved the start dates of federal terms.
Snyder v. Phelps held the First Amendment shielded Westboro Baptist Church from tort liability for its picketing.

03-04.text: Congress passed the Eleventh Amendment and sent it to the states for ratification.

03-05.text: British soldiers fired on a crowd at the Boston Customs House, the event remembered as the Boston Massacre.

03-06.text: Mexican forces launched the final assault on the Alamo, and its defenders fell.

03-09.text: Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire described "fighting words" as a category of unprotected speech.
New York Times Co. v. Sullivan adopted the "actual malice" standard for public officials' libel suits.
03-09.case: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964)

03-16.text: James Madison, chief drafter of the Bill of Rights, was born.
The Convention of 1836 adopted the Constitution of the Republic of Texas around midnight and elected an interim government.

03-18.text: Gideon v. Wainwright held that States must appoint counsel for indigent defendants charged with felonies.

03-21.text: Congress passed the Twenty-second Amendment limiting presidential elections to two.
Caetano v. Massachusetts vacated a ruling upholding a stun gun ban because its reasoning conflicted with Heller.

03-23.text: Congress passed the Twenty-sixth Amendment lowering the voting age to 18.

03-25.text: Torres v. Madrid held applying physical force to the body with intent to restrain is a seizure even if the person does not submit.

03-26.text: Florida v. Jardines held a drug-dog investigation on a home's front porch was a Fourth Amendment search.
Bondi v. VanDerStok held the ATF rule on weapon parts kits is not facially inconsistent with the Gun Control Act.

03-27.text: On Palm Sunday, about 342 men of James W. Fannin's command were executed in the Goliad Massacre.
Tennessee v. Garner held deadly force may not be used to stop a fleeing suspect unless necessary and the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious injury.

03-29.text: The Twenty-third Amendment was ratified, giving the District of Columbia electors in presidential elections.

04-03.text: Smith v. Allwright held excluding Black voters from the Texas Democratic primary unconstitutional.

04-04.text: Thompson v. Clark held a malicious prosecution plaintiff need not show the prosecution ended with an affirmative indication of innocence.

04-06.text: Mexico enacted the Law of April 6, 1830, restricting Anglo-American immigration into Texas.

04-08.text: The Seventeenth Amendment was ratified, providing for direct popular election of U.S. Senators.

04-13.text: Thomas Jefferson, principal author of the Declaration of Independence, was born.

04-17.text: Missouri v. McNeely was decided on warrantless blood draws in drunk-driving cases.

04-19.text: The Battles of Lexington and Concord began the armed conflict of the American Revolution.

04-20.text: President Grant signed the Civil Rights Act of 1871, whose Section 1 created the civil action now codified at 42 U.S.C. 1983.
Ramos v. Louisiana, a Sixth Amendment case on unanimous jury verdicts in state criminal trials, was decided.

04-21.text: Texans under Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna's army at San Jacinto in about eighteen minutes, ending the Texas Revolution.
Arizona v. Gant limited vehicle searches incident to a recent occupant's arrest.

04-26.text: United States v. Lopez held the Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeded Congress's Commerce Clause authority.

04-30.text: George Washington delivered his first inaugural address as the first President under the Constitution.
Batson v. Kentucky was decided on race-based peremptory strikes of jurors.

05-03.text: Hernandez v. Texas held excluding jurors because of ancestry or national origin violates the Fourteenth Amendment.

05-07.text: The Twenty-seventh Amendment on congressional pay was ratified, about 203 years after it was first proposed in 1789.

05-13.text: Congress passed the Seventeenth Amendment for the direct election of Senators.
Brady v. Maryland held prosecutors' suppression of material evidence favorable to an accused, on request, violates due process.

05-14.text: The Federal Convention convened at the State House (Independence Hall) in Philadelphia.
At Velasco, Texas officials had the captured Santa Anna sign two treaties, one public and one secret.
Strickland v. Washington set the two-part test (deficient performance and prejudice) for ineffective assistance claims.

05-15.text: United States v. Miller held the Court could not take judicial notice that a short-barreled shotgun had militia relevance.
Graham v. Connor held excessive force claims in an arrest or stop are judged by Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness.

05-17.text: Brown v. Board of Education held racial segregation in public schools violates the Equal Protection Clause.
05-17.case: Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954)

05-17.text: Caniglia v. Strom rejected extending the "community caretaking" rationale to warrantless searches of the home.

05-18.text: Plessy v. Ferguson upheld "separate but equal" railroad accommodations; Brown v. Board later rejected the doctrine in schools.

05-19.text: May 19, 1986 is the cutoff date in the federal machine gun possession ban added by the Firearm Owners Protection Act.

05-20.text: Duncan v. Louisiana held the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees jury trial in state criminal cases where the Sixth would apply.

05-28.text: Nieves v. Bartlett held a retaliatory arrest claim generally fails where there was probable cause to arrest.

05-29.text: Patrick Henry, Virginia patriot and orator, was born.

05-30.text: NRA v. Vullo held the NRA plausibly alleged a First Amendment violation by a state official coercing regulated entities.
05-30.case: National Rifle Assn. of America v. Vullo, 602 U.S. 175 (2024)

06-01.text: Near v. Minnesota struck down a prior restraint on a newspaper reporting official misconduct.

06-04.text: Congress passed the Nineteenth Amendment protecting women's right to vote.

06-05.text: Sweatt v. Painter held equal protection required admitting the petitioner to the University of Texas Law School.
Smith & Wesson v. Mexico held the PLCAA bars Mexico's suit because it did not plausibly allege the manufacturers aided and abetted illegal sales.
06-05.case: Smith & Wesson Brands, Inc. v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos, 605 U.S. 280 (2025)

06-06.text: Monell held local governments may be sued under 42 U.S.C. 1983 when their own policy or custom causes a violation, partly overruling Monroe v. Pape.
06-06.case: Monell v. Dept. of Social Services, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)

06-07.text: Richard Henry Lee introduced the Lee Resolution in Congress, calling for independence.
Cohen v. California reversed a conviction for wearing a jacket with an expletive protesting the draft.

06-09.text: Brandenburg v. Ohio protected advocacy of force unless directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.

06-10.text: Terry v. Ohio allowed a limited weapons frisk when specific facts lead an officer to reasonably conclude a person is armed and dangerous.

06-11.text: Congress appointed the Committee of Five to draft a declaration of independence.
United States v. Eichman held prosecution under the federal Flag Protection Act inconsistent with the First Amendment.
Kyllo v. United States held aiming a thermal imager, a device not in general public use, at a home is a search requiring a warrant.

06-12.text: Loving v. Virginia struck down Virginia's interracial marriage ban under the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses.

06-13.text: Congress passed the Fourteenth Amendment, including its Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses.
Miranda v. Arizona required procedural safeguards before statements from custodial interrogation may be used.

06-14.text: The Continental Congress approved a design for the national flag.
West Virginia v. Barnette held a compulsory school flag salute violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments.
06-14.case: West Virginia State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624 (1943)

06-14.text: Garland v. Cargill held ATF exceeded its statutory authority by classifying a bump stock as a "machinegun."

06-15.text: The Twelfth Amendment was ratified, requiring electors to cast separate ballots for President and Vice President.

06-16.text: Congress passed the Twenty-third Amendment on presidential electors for the District of Columbia.

06-17.text: The Battle of Bunker Hill was fought during the Siege of Boston.
Juneteenth National Independence Day became a federal holiday when the President signed the bill into law.

06-19.text: At Galveston, Union General Gordon Granger issued General Order No. 3 announcing that "all slaves are free."
Mapp v. Ohio held evidence from unconstitutional searches is inadmissible in state criminal trials.
Packingham v. North Carolina struck down a law barring sex offenders from social networking sites as a violation of the First Amendment.

06-20.text: Gonzalez v. Trevino held the Fifth Circuit took an overly cramped view of the Nieves exception.

06-21.text: Bivens recognized a damages action against federal agents for violating the Fourth Amendment.
06-21.case: Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)

06-21.text: Texas v. Johnson held a Texas flag desecration conviction inconsistent with the First Amendment.
United States v. Rahimi held a person found by a court to pose a credible threat to another's safety may be temporarily disarmed.

06-22.text: Escobedo v. Illinois was decided on a suspect's right to counsel during police interrogation.
Carpenter v. United States held acquiring historical cell-site records is a Fourth Amendment search.

06-23.text: Chimel v. California limited a search incident to arrest to the arrestee's person and area within reach.
Lange v. California held pursuit of a fleeing misdemeanor suspect does not categorically justify warrantless home entry.
Mahanoy Area School District v. B. L. held a school's interests did not outweigh a student's off-campus speech in that case.
06-23.case: Mahanoy Area School Dist. v. B. L., 594 U.S. 180 (2021)

06-23.text: NYSRPA v. Bruen held New York's "proper cause" requirement for public carry licenses violates the Second and Fourteenth Amendments.
06-23.case: New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn., Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022)

06-23.text: Vega v. Tekoh held a violation of the Miranda rules does not provide a basis for a Section 1983 claim.

06-25.text: Riley v. California held police generally need a warrant to search digital data on an arrestee's cell phone.

06-26.text: Reno v. ACLU held key Communications Decency Act provisions abridged the freedom of speech.
06-26.case: Reno v. American Civil Liberties Union, 521 U.S. 844 (1997)

06-26.text: District of Columbia v. Heller held the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess a firearm unconnected with militia service.
06-26.case: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008)

06-27.text: Printz v. United States struck down the Brady Act's interim command that local officers conduct background checks.
Hope v. Pelzer held prison guards were not entitled to qualified immunity for hitching-post treatment.
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District held the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses protected a coach's personal prayer.
06-27.case: Kennedy v. Bremerton School Dist., 597 U.S. 507 (2022)

06-28.text: McDonald v. City of Chicago held the Second Amendment right recognized in Heller applies to the States.
06-28.case: McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010)

06-30.text: NAACP v. Alabama protected the NAACP's membership lists from compelled disclosure to the State.
06-30.case: NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, 357 U.S. 449 (1958)

07-01.text: The Twenty-sixth Amendment was ratified, setting the minimum voting age at 18.

07-02.text: The Continental Congress adopted the Lee Resolution for independence, with 12 of 13 colonies voting in favor.
Congress passed the Sixteenth Amendment, the federal income tax amendment.
President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

07-04.text: The Continental Congress formally adopted the Declaration of Independence.
A Texas convention in Austin approved annexation to the United States by a vote of 55 to 1.

07-06.text: Congress passed the Twenty-fifth Amendment on presidential succession and disability.

07-09.text: The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified, guaranteeing citizenship, due process and equal protection of the laws.

07-19.text: Congress ordered the Declaration of Independence engrossed on parchment for signing.

08-02.text: Most members of Congress signed the engrossed parchment copy of the Declaration of Independence.

08-06.text: President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which outlawed literacy tests as a voting prerequisite.

08-18.text: The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified, barring denial of the right to vote on account of sex.

08-27.text: Congress passed the Twenty-fourth Amendment banning poll taxes in federal elections.

09-01.text: The Texas Firearm Carry Act (HB 1927) took effect, allowing eligible adults 21 and older to carry a handgun without a license.

09-03.text: The Treaty of Paris was signed, ending the Revolutionary War.

09-06.text: The Texas Constitutional Convention of 1875 met in Austin to write a new state constitution.

09-17.text: Delegates signed the U.S. Constitution at the Federal Convention in Philadelphia.

09-20.text: Mexican General Cos landed 500 men at Copano Bay, a step toward the opening of the Texas Revolution.

09-22.text: President Lincoln issued the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

09-25.text: The First Congress proposed 12 amendments to the states; ten became the Bill of Rights and one later became the 27th Amendment.

10-02.text: Texian colonists at Gonzales refused to surrender their cannon under a "Come and Take It" flag, the first battle of the Texas Revolution.

10-03.text: The First Congress of the Republic of Texas assembled at Columbia.

10-13.text: Texas voters approved annexation and adopted the proposed state constitution.

10-14.text: About 300 Texian volunteers under Stephen F. Austin began moving toward San Antonio.

10-22.text: Sam Houston took the oath of office as president of the Republic of Texas.

11-02.text: Taylor v. Riojas held prison officers were not entitled to qualified immunity for obviously unconstitutional cell conditions.

11-07.text: Powell v. Alabama was decided on criminal defendants' right to counsel.

11-15.text: The Continental Congress adopted the Articles of Confederation.

12-05.text: The Twenty-first Amendment was ratified, repealing the Eighteenth Amendment and ending national Prohibition.

12-06.text: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified, abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for crime.

12-09.text: Congress passed the Twelfth Amendment, changing how electors vote for President and Vice President.

12-15.text: The Bill of Rights was ratified when three-fourths of the state legislatures approved the ten amendments.

12-18.text: Congress passed the Eighteenth Amendment on Prohibition.
Katz v. United States, a landmark Fourth Amendment privacy case, was decided.

12-23.text: George Washington resigned his commission as commander in chief of the Continental Army.

12-29.text: Texas legally entered the Union when Congress accepted its state constitution.

09-12.text: The Supreme Court decided Cooper v. Aaron, a school desegregation case.
